lessons.title: Normal areas, notation and interpretation
lessons.summary: Read normal parameters and turn continuous events into correctly standardised areas.
lessons.objective: Read normal parameters and turn continuous events into correctly standardised areas.
lessons.before: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.
lessons.ideas:
Density height is not point probability

A continuous model assigns probabilities to intervals through areas under its density curve. The total area is one. A single exact value has probability zero, so including or excluding an endpoint does not change a continuous area. A recorded value rounded to a unit represents an interval and can have positive probability.

Mean and variance have different roles

\[X\sim\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2),\qquad\sigma>0.\]

The mean locates the centre. The standard deviation controls spread; the variance is its square. Curves with smaller standard deviation are narrower and taller, but all have area one. For a common centre, a fixed central interval contains more probability under the narrower curve.

Standardise by the standard deviation

\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma}\sim\mathrm N(0,1).\]

Subtract the mean and divide by σ, not σ². A value below the mean has a negative z-score. Standardise both ends of an interval separately and show the substitutions.

Use a consistent cumulative convention

Write Φ(z)=P(Z≤z). A left tail is Φ(z); a right tail is 1−Φ(z). Symmetry gives Φ(−z)=1−Φ(z).

\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(a<X<b)&=\Phi\!\left(\frac{b-\mu}{\sigma}\right)\\&\quad-\Phi\!\left(\frac{a-\mu}{\sigma}\right).\end{aligned}\]

A table giving area between zero and z needs conversion to this cumulative convention. A quick sketch checks whether the probability should be above or below one half.

Read rounding intervals as intervals

If a value is recorded to the nearest whole unit as r, its underlying value lies from r−0.5 to r+0.5, apart from endpoint conventions of zero probability. Do not confuse this with an exact reading X=r.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
mistakes: The second normal parameter is variance, not standard deviation.
Subtract the lower cumulative probability from the upper one.
A right tail is not the left cumulative area.
An exact point and a rounded recording are different events.

examples.title: Read variance, then standardise
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(72,25)\). Give its standard deviation, the exact z-score for X=78, and \(\mathrm P(X>78)\).
examples.solution:
Take the positive square root of the variance. Standardise by this standard deviation and complement the lower cumulative area.

\[\begin{aligned}z_a&=\frac{78-72}{5},\\{}z_a&\approx1.2000.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X>78)&\approx0.1151.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Standard deviation: \(5\).

Exact z-score: \(\frac{6}{5}\).

Right-tail probability (4 d.p.): \(0.1151\).

lessons.title: Quantiles and unknown parameters
lessons.summary: Recover cutoffs, means and standard deviations from lower-tail probabilities and independent equations.
lessons.objective: Recover cutoffs, means and standard deviations from lower-tail probabilities and independent equations.
lessons.before: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.
lessons.ideas:
Convert every probability to a lower tail first

If P(X≤c)=p, use z=Φ⁻¹(p), then c=μ+σz. For an upper-tail probability α use p=1−α. A lower quantile below the median must have a negative z-score.

\[c=\mu+\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p).\]

A known standard deviation leaves a linear equation for the mean

\[\mu=a-\sigma\Phi^{-1}(p).\]

Use the actual stated cumulative probability. Keep the z-score at calculator precision while recovering μ, then use the recovered parameters for any follow-on area.

A known mean determines the standard deviation

\[\sigma=\frac{a-\mu}{\Phi^{-1}(p)}.\]

The numerator and z-score must have compatible signs so σ is positive. A negative result is a reason to check the tail and sign, not to silently take an absolute value. Square σ only when the variance is required.

Two probability statements give two equations

\[\begin{aligned}a&=\mu+\sigma z_a,\\b&=\mu+\sigma z_b.\end{aligned}\]

Subtract to eliminate μ. The difference in physical cutoffs corresponds to the difference in z-scores. Recover σ first, then μ, and check both original probabilities. Equal tail probabilities for different cutoffs would not determine a positive spread.

Rounding is the final step

Rounding an intermediate quantile can move the final cutoff or parameter. Record the equations and retain full precision internally. Label whether your final answer is a standard deviation or a variance.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
mistakes: An upper-tail percentage must be complemented before inverse normal.
A lower quantile can require a negative z-score.
Do not replace a negative inferred standard deviation by its absolute value.
Use two independent equations to determine both parameters.

examples.title: A cumulative probability determines a cutoff
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find the standard-normal quantile z and cutoff c such that \(\mathrm P(X\le c)\)=0.95.
examples.solution:
The probability is already a lower cumulative probability. Use inverse normal, then undo standardisation.

\[\begin{aligned}z&=\Phi^{-1}(0.95),\\{}z&\approx1.6449,\\{}c&=80+6z,\\{}c&\approx89.87.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Standard-normal quantile (4 d.p.): \(1.6449\).

Cutoff c (2 d.p.): \(89.87\).

examples.title: Recover a mean from a known spread
examples.question: X is normal with standard deviation 5 and \(\mathrm P(X\le 70)\)=0.1. Find the mean and \(\mathrm P(70
examples.solution:
Write the lower-tail z-score equation and solve for the mean. Use the unrounded recovered mean in the new interval.

\[\begin{aligned}z&=\Phi^{-1}(0.1),\\{}\mu&=70-5z,\\{}\mu&\approx76.41,\\{}\mathrm P(\text{interval})&\approx0.7683.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Mean (2 d.p.): \(76.41\).

Follow-on interval probability (4 d.p.): \(0.7683\).

examples.title: Recover a positive standard deviation
examples.question: X is normal with mean 80, and \(\mathrm P(X>90)\)=0.05. Find the standard deviation, the variance, and \(\mathrm P(75
examples.solution:
Convert the right tail to a lower tail before inverse normal. Divide the displacement by its z-score, checking the positive standard deviation. Retain the unrounded value for the variance and follow-on interval.

\[\begin{aligned}z&=\Phi^{-1}(0.95),\\{}\sigma&=\frac{10}{z},\\{}\sigma&\approx6.08,\\{}\sigma^2&\approx36.96,\\{}\mathrm P(\text{interval})&\approx0.7005.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Standard deviation (2 d.p.): \(6.08\).

Variance (2 d.p.): \(36.96\).

Follow-on interval probability (4 d.p.): \(0.7005\).

examples.title: Two quantiles determine two parameters
examples.question: X is normal, \(\mathrm P(X\le 60)\)=0.15 and \(\mathrm P(X\le 84)\)=0.85. Find its mean and standard deviation, then \(\mathrm P(60
examples.solution:
Obtain two z-scores. Subtract the two standardisation equations, recover the positive spread, then substitute for the mean. The final interval is also the difference of the two given cumulative probabilities.

\[\begin{aligned}z_a&=\Phi^{-1}(0.15),\\{}z_b&=\Phi^{-1}(0.85),\\{}60&=\mu+\sigma z_a,\\{}84&=\mu+\sigma z_b,\\{}\sigma&\approx11.58,\\{}\mu&\approx72.00,\\{}\mathrm P(\text{interval})&=0.7.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Mean (2 d.p.): \(72.00\).

Standard deviation (2 d.p.): \(11.58\).

Probability between the stated cutoffs (4 d.p.): \(0.7000\).

lessons.title: Conditional and repeated normal models
lessons.summary: Keep conditions and route weights explicit when normal areas feed further probability models.
lessons.objective: Keep conditions and route weights explicit when normal areas feed further probability models.
lessons.before: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.
lessons.ideas:
Condition on the stated region

For a condition H, divide the probability of the intersection by P(H). If b>a, then X>b already implies X>a.

\[\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)=\frac{\mathrm P(X>b)}{\mathrm P(X>a)}.\]

Using the unconditional right tail alone ignores the smaller conditional sample space.

An interval probability can be a binomial success probability

First calculate q for one normal reading meeting its criterion. If n readings are independent with the same distribution, the number meeting that criterion is B(n,q). Use the unrounded q in the second stage, not a rounded z-score or the original cutoff.

A mixture is assembled by routes

If a machine is selected before a reading, multiply each machine’s event probability by its selection probability and add. For a posterior machine probability, retain the relevant route as the numerator. A mixture of two normal distributions is not generally one normal distribution with averaged parameters.

A rounded condition needs its own physical boundary

For nearest-unit recording, recorded X≥k corresponds to the underlying value being at least k−0.5. Intersect this with any requested recorded interval before conditioning. This rounding interval describes a measurement; it is distinct from approximating a discrete count by a continuous normal model.

Expected frequencies are long-run quantities

For n comparable readings and a single-reading event probability q, the expected count is nq. It need not be an integer. Round it only if the question explicitly asks for a rounded count.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
mistakes: A conditional denominator is the condition probability.
Use an unrounded single-reading probability in a repeated model.
A normal mixture does not generally reduce to averaged parameters.
A rounded threshold changes the boundary by half a recording unit.

examples.title: The larger tail is the conditioning space
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find \(\mathrm P(X>80)\), \(\mathrm P(X>89)\), and \(\mathrm P(X>89 \mid X>80)\).
examples.solution:
The smaller upper-tail event lies wholly inside the condition. Standardise each cutoff, then divide the intersection probability by the condition probability.

\[\begin{aligned}z_a&=\frac{80-80}{6},\\{}z_a&\approx0.0000,\\{}z_b&=\frac{89-80}{6},\\{}z_b&\approx1.5000.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)&=\frac{\mathrm P(X>b)}{\mathrm P(X>a)},\\{}\mathrm P(X>b\mid X>a)&\approx0.1336.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Condition probability (4 d.p.): \(0.5000\).

Intersection probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0668\).

Conditional probability (4 d.p.): \(0.1336\).

examples.title: A normal tail becomes a repeated-trial success
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Take 3 independent readings and let K count those above 86. Find the single-reading probability q, \(\mathrm P(K=2)\) and \(\mathrm E(K)\).
examples.solution:
Compute the normal right tail first. Independence and an identical reading distribution then give a binomial count with that unrounded probability.

\[\begin{aligned}z_a&=\frac{86-80}{6},\\{}z_a&\approx1.0000.\end{aligned}\]\[K\sim\mathrm B(3,q).\]\[\begin{aligned}q&\approx0.1587,\\{}\mathrm P(K=2)&\approx0.0635,\\{}\mathrm E(K)&\approx0.48.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Single-reading probability (4 d.p.): \(0.1587\).

Repeated-count probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0635\).

Expected qualifying readings (2 d.p.): \(0.48\).

examples.title: Retain route weights for a posterior
examples.question: For each reading choose machine A with probability 0.6, otherwise B. A readings are \(\mathrm N(70,25)\); B readings are \(\mathrm N(80,36)\). Find the probability a reading is below 76, the probability it came from A given it is below 76, and the expected number below 76 in 120 independent repetitions of this selection process.
examples.solution:
Let H mean the reading is below the cutoff, and let \(q_A\), \(q_B\) be its probability under each machine. Weight the lower tails by their route probabilities. Keep only the A route for the posterior numerator.

\[\begin{aligned}q_A&\approx0.8849,\\{}q_B&\approx0.2525,\\{}q&=0.6q_A+0.4q_B,\\{}q&\approx0.6320,\\{}\mathrm P(A\mid H)&\approx0.8402,\\{}\mathrm E(K)&\approx75.83.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Overall event probability (4 d.p.): \(0.6320\).

Machine A given the event (4 d.p.): \(0.8402\).

Expected event count (2 d.p.): \(75.83\).

examples.title: Condition on the physical rounding boundary
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm N(80,36)\). Record X to the nearest whole unit as R. Give the exact underlying boundary for R≥76, \(\mathrm P(R=80)\), and \(\mathrm P(R=80 \mid R\ge 76)\); then choose the correct point/recording statement.
examples.solution:
The condition starts half a unit below its smallest allowed recorded integer. The requested recording interval lies inside this condition, so divide its normal area by the corrected upper tail.

\[\begin{aligned}a&=\frac{151}{2},\\{}\mathrm P(R=80)&\approx0.0664,\\{}\mathrm P(R=80\mid R\ge76)&\approx0.0859.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Exact conditioning boundary: \(\frac{151}{2}\).

Recorded-value probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0664\).

Conditional recorded-value probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0859\).

Correct conclusion: An exact X-value has probability zero, but a rounded recording represents an interval.

lessons.title: Normal approximation and continuity correction
lessons.summary: Check the approximation conditions and convert exact integer events to continuous strips.
lessons.objective: Check the approximation conditions and convert exact integer events to continuous strips.
lessons.before: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.
lessons.ideas:
Check both expected counts

For X~B(n,p), this syllabus uses a normal approximation when n is sufficiently large that both np>5 and n(1−p)>5. Equality to 5 does not meet the stated strict criterion. Independence and a common p must still justify the underlying binomial model.

\[Y\sim\mathrm N\bigl(np,np(1-p)\bigr).\]

The second parameter is variance. Standardisation divides by the square root of that variance.

An integer occupies a unit-width strip

Continuity correction replaces the mass at integer k by the area from k−0.5 to k+0.5. Sketch the bars or a number line first.

\[\begin{aligned}X\ge k&\longrightarrow Y>k-0.5,\\X\le k&\longrightarrow Y<k+0.5,\\X>k&\longrightarrow Y>k+0.5,\\X<k&\longrightarrow Y<k-0.5.\end{aligned}\]

Translate strict intervals before correcting

For integer bounds L and U, the event L<X<U contains L+1 through U−1. Its continuous strip starts at L+0.5 and ends at U−0.5. Do not move both boundaries in the same direction.

The result remains an approximation

A normal answer need not equal the exact binomial probability. State the approximating distribution, corrected interval, z-scores and approximate area. Do not add a continuity correction to a quantity already modelled as a genuinely continuous normal reading.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
mistakes: Both np and n(1−p) must exceed 5 under the stated criterion.
Use the standard deviation sqrt(np(1−p)).
Exactly k requires a strip, not the zero-area point Y=k.
An approximation is not an exact binomial calculation.

examples.title: Check both strict expected-count conditions
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(80,\frac{2}{5})\). Give np and n(1−p), then decide whether both strict expected-count conditions for the normal approximation are met.
examples.solution:
Calculate both expected counts and compare each with 5 using a strict inequality.

\[\begin{aligned}np&=32,\\{}n(1-p)&=48.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Exact expected successes: \(32\).

Exact expected failures: \(48\).

Correct conclusion: Both expected counts exceed 5, so the stated criterion is met.

examples.title: Correct an inclusive upper tail
examples.question: \(X\sim\mathrm B(120,\frac{1}{4})\). Give the exact corrected boundary for \(\mathrm P(X\ge 35)\), its z-score, and the normal approximation to that probability.
examples.solution:
Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

\[Y\sim\mathrm N(30,\frac{45}{2}).\]\[\begin{aligned}a&=\frac{69}{2},\\{}z&\approx0.9487,\\{}\mathrm P(X\ge35)&\approx0.1714.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Exact corrected boundary: \(\frac{69}{2}\).

Corrected z-score (4 d.p.): \(0.9487\).

Normal-approximated upper tail (4 d.p.): \(0.1714\).

lessons.title: Multi-stage models and inverse problems
lessons.summary: Connect parameter recovery, integer design limits and reward decisions without importing Statistics 2 rules.
lessons.objective: Connect parameter recovery, integer design limits and reward decisions without importing Statistics 2 rules.
lessons.before: Use continuous areas, conditional probability and binomial moments from the preceding chapters. In \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), the second parameter is variance. Give probabilities to 4 decimal places and estimated measurements to 2 decimal places when labelled; calculator precision is also accepted. Exact boundary and integer fields remain exact. Written problems keep their own rounding instructions.
lessons.ideas:
Recover a binomial model before approximating it

If its mean and variance are given, recover p and integer n using the preceding chapter. Verify both expected counts exceed 5 before using a normal approximation. Apply continuity correction only to the final count event.

A continuous cutoff can imply an integer design decision

Find the real quantile first. If an integer cutoff must make a lower-tail probability at least the target, choose the smallest integer satisfying the original condition and check its predecessor. A displayed rounded quantile is not a substitute for this integer check.

A normal event can trigger a discrete reward

First calculate the normal probability q of the triggering event. Build the finite reward table, then find its weighted expectation and variance. This uses the previous discrete-distribution chapter; it does not assume Statistics 2 formulae for arbitrary linear combinations of normal variables.

Relationships between parameters are extra equations

If σ=cμ with μ>0, substitute into the standardised probability equation. Solve for μ and then obtain the positive σ. Check the original tail. Keep the original positive-parameter restriction throughout.

A normal model has an unbounded support

Even when a real measurement cannot be negative, its normal model may assign a small negative-tail probability. That is a limitation to assess in context, not a reason to set the model probability to zero. Distinguish an unrounded small probability from a displayed probability rounded to four decimals.
lessons.method:
1. Identify the mean, variance and positive standard deviation.
  2. Sketch and label the requested region before choosing a tail or interval.
  3. Standardise each boundary using the standard deviation.
  4. Use a cumulative normal probability or inverse cumulative probability with the correct tail.
  5. For counts, check approximation conditions and apply continuity correction to the integer event.
  6. For a condition, restrict the numerator and denominator; retain full precision until the final answer.
mistakes: Check feasibility of inferred binomial parameters before approximation.
Integer cutoffs require a neighbouring-integer check.
A two-level reward uses a discrete probability table.
A very small normal tail is not mathematically zero.

examples.title: Infer a count model before approximating
examples.question: A binomial X has mean 40 and variance 20. Recover its n and p, then give the exact continuity-corrected boundary and a normal approximation to \(\mathrm P(X\ge 45)\).

Both expected counts exceed 5. Use the binomial mean and variance for the normal model, then divide corrected displacements by its standard deviation. This is an approximate area, not the exact binomial probability.

\[Y\sim\mathrm N(40,20).\]\[\begin{aligned}a&=\frac{89}{2},\\{}z&\approx1.0062,\\{}\mathrm P(X\ge45)&\approx0.1572.\end{aligned}\]

Exact binomial success probability: \(\frac{1}{2}\).

Exact corrected boundary: \(\frac{89}{2}\).

Normal-approximated upper tail (4 d.p.): \(0.1572\).

examples.title: A parameter relationship closes the model
examples.question: X is normal with positive mean μ and standard deviation σ=\(\frac{1}{3}\)μ. Given \(\mathrm P(X>40)\)=0.1, find μ, σ and \(\mathrm P(X<0)\), then choose the correct model interpretation.
examples.solution:
Convert the upper tail to a cumulative quantile and substitute the given relation for σ. The normal model still has a negative tail; a displayed rounded zero is not a mathematical assertion of zero probability.

\[\begin{aligned}z&=\Phi^{-1}(0.9),\\{}40&=\mu(1+cz),\\{}\mu&\approx28.03,\\{}\sigma&\approx9.34,\\{}\mathrm P(X<0)&\approx0.0013.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Mean (2 d.p.): \(28.03\).

Standard deviation (2 d.p.): \(9.34\).

Negative-tail probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0013\).

Correct conclusion: The normal model can assign a small negative tail even when physical values are non-negative.

questions.title: Read variance, then standardise
questions.prompt_html: \(X\sim\mathrm N(50,16)\). Give its standard deviation, the exact z-score for X=54, and \(\mathrm P(X>54)\).
questions.solution_html:
Take the positive square root of the variance. Standardise by this standard deviation and complement the lower cumulative area.

\[\begin{aligned}z_a&=\frac{54-50}{4},\\{}z_a&\approx1.0000.\end{aligned}\]\[\begin{aligned}\mathrm P(X>54)&\approx0.1587.\end{aligned}\]

Complete answers

Mean (2 d.p.): \(41.31\).

Standard deviation (2 d.p.): \(10.33\).

Negative-tail probability (4 d.p.): \(0.0000\).

questions.title: Preparing a measuring instrument
questions.prompt_html:
The preparation time \(T\), in minutes, for an instrument is normally distributed with mean \(26\) and standard deviation \(3.2\).

  1. Find the probability that a preparation takes more than \(30\) minutes.

    [3]

  2. For \(180\) such preparations, estimate the number taking less than \(23\) minutes. Give your estimate to the nearest whole number.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(T>30)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z>\frac{30-26}{3.2}\right)=1-\Phi(1.25)=0.106.\]

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(T<23)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z<\frac{23-26}{3.2}\right)=\Phi(-0.9375)=0.174.\]\[\text{expected number}=180\Phi\!\left(\frac{23-26}{3.2}\right)=31.365128.\]

Round only the final expected number: \(31\).
questions.hint_html: The expected count uses the probability of being below the second limit, not the probability calculated in part (a).

A reading of \(72\) corresponds to \(71.5\leq X<72.5\). Exact halfway values have probability zero in a continuous model.

\[\mathrm P(X>74.5)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z>\frac{74.5-72.4}{2.2}\right)=1-\Phi(0.95455)=0.170.\]

questions.title: A mean linked to the standard deviation
questions.prompt_html:
The variable \(X\) is normally distributed with mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\), where \(\mu=1.5\sigma\) and \(\sigma>0\).

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that \(X\) differs from its mean by less than \(0.7\mu\).

    [3]

\[Z=\frac{X-\mu}{\sigma},\qquad\frac{2\mu-\mu}{\sigma}=1.5.\]\[\mathrm P(X>2\mu)=1-\Phi(1.5)=0.0668.\]

(b)

The relation and the positive standard deviation imply \(\mu>0\), so this is a positive distance.

\[\mathrm P(|X-\mu|<0.7\mu)=\mathrm P(|Z|<1.05)=2\Phi(1.05)-1=0.706.\]

questions.title: A tolerance centred on the mean
questions.prompt_html:
A measurement \(X\) units is modelled by \(\mathrm N(81,4.2^2)\). It is acceptable when its actual value differs from the mean by no more than \(3.8\) units. A random sample contains \(420\) measurements.

  1. Estimate the number of acceptable measurements, to the nearest whole number.

    [4]

  2. A student adds 0.5 to each tolerance limit before standardising. Explain why this is not appropriate here.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(266\).

(b)

The event is defined for the actual continuous measurement, not a rounded reading or a discrete count. No continuity correction is required.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\mathrm P(|X-81|\leq 3.8)=2\Phi\!\left(\frac{3.8}{4.2}\right)-1=0.634.\]\[\text{expected number}=420\times 0.634408462=266.451554.\]

This rounds to \(266\).

(b)

A continuity correction approximates the area of discrete count bars using a continuous variable. These limits already describe an event for a continuous variable; moving them changes the event.

questions.title: Assessing a normal model
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Rounding intervals and data interpretation.

A positive response time \(X\) seconds is provisionally modelled by \(\mathrm N(18,25)\). A large exploratory sample has lower quartile \(13\), median \(18\) and upper quartile \(28\) seconds.

  1. Calculate the probability of a negative response time under this model.

    [3]

  2. Find the lower and upper quartiles predicted by the normal model.

    [2]

  3. Comment on the suitability of the normal model, using both the negative-time probability and the sample quartiles. A formal statistical test is not required.

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.000159\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

\(14.6,\quad 21.4\) seconds.

(c)

The negative-time probability is small, so impossible values alone need not make the approximation useless. However, the observed unequal distances from the median to the two quartiles suggest asymmetry and cast doubt on this particular normal model.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X<0)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z<\frac{0-18}{5}\right)=\Phi(-3.6)=0.000159.\]

(b)

\[Q_1=18+5\Phi^{-1}(0.25)=14.6,\qquad Q_3=18+5\Phi^{-1}(0.75)=21.4.\]

(c)

A normal model has equally spaced quartiles about its median. Here the observed distances are \(5\) and \(10\). This is descriptive evidence against symmetry, not a proof from a sample or a formal hypothesis test.
questions.hint_html: A small impossible-value probability and a symmetric shape are different checks on a model.

questions.prompt_html:
The lengths \(X\) mm of a type of manufactured strip are modelled by a normal distribution. In a random sample of \(500\) strips, \(80\) have length below \(42\) mm and \(55\) have length above \(65\) mm.

    [5]

    [3]

(a)

\[\widehat{\mathrm P}(X<42)=\frac{80}{500}=0.16,\qquad\widehat{\mathrm P}(X<65)=1-\frac{55}{500}=0.89.\]\[\frac{42-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.16)=-0.994458,\qquad\frac{65-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.89)=1.226528.\]

Subtract the first equation from the second before finding the mean. Keep the signs of both quantiles.

Unrounded values are retained in the following calculations.

\[\mathrm P(|X-\mu|>1.5\sigma)=2[1-\Phi(1.5)]=0.134.\]\[\text{expected number}=1500\times0.133614403=200.421604.\]

The final estimate is \(200\).

questions.prompt_html:
The variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm N(\mu,\sigma^2)\), where \(\sigma>0\). It is given that \(3\mu=2\sigma^2\) and \(\mathrm P(X<0.5\mu)=0.22\).

  2. Find \(w>0\) such that \(\mathrm P(\mu-w<X<\mu+w)=0.8\).

The recovered standard deviation is positive; the zero value is not permitted.

(b)

The total excluded probability is split equally between the tails.

\[\frac w\sigma=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(\frac{1+0.8}2\right),\qquad w=2.97.\]

questions.prompt_html:
The random variable \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm N(86,64)\).

  1. Find \(b\) such that \(\mathrm P(78<X<b)=0.55\).

    [2]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(90.4\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

No. The largest possible area above the lower boundary is only \(0.841\), which is less than \(0.95\).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

(b)

\[\mathrm P(78<X<c)<\mathrm P(X>78)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{78-86}{8}\right)=0.841.\]

Even allowing the upper endpoint to tend to infinity cannot reach the requested area.

questions.title: A two-stage grading rule
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability.

An optical measurement \(X\) is normally distributed with mean \(54\) and standard deviation \(8\). A measurement below \(43\) is graded C. The remaining measurements are divided into grades A and B, with A assigned to the highest measurements. Among measurements not graded C, the ratio of grade A to grade B is \(3:5\).

  1. Find the proportion graded C.

    [2]

  2. Find the lower boundary for grade A.

    [3]

  3. Given that a measurement exceeds the mean, find the probability that it is graded A.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X<43)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z<\frac{43-54}{8}\right)=\Phi(-1.375)=0.0846.\]

(b)

questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability; Binomial models and moments.

A component dimension \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm N(100,36)\). It passes inspection when \(92<X<108\). A set consists of \(4\) independently produced components.

    [3]

  2. Given that the set contains at least one failed component, find the probability that it contains exactly one failed component.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

Standardise using \(Z=\frac{X-100}{6}\).

(b)

\[\mathrm P(\text{exactly one fail})=4(1-q)q^{3}=0.399.\]\[\mathrm P(\text{exactly one fail}\mid\text{at least one fail})=\frac{4(1-q)q^{3}}{1-q^{4}}=0.721.\]

questions.title: Finding a large reading
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments; Logarithms and integer probability bounds.

A reading \(X\) is normally distributed with mean \(68\) and standard deviation \(7\). A reading greater than \(77\) is called large. All readings are independent.

  1. Find the probability that fewer than two of \(7\) readings are large.

    [3]

  2. Find the least integer \(n\) for which the probability of at least one large reading in \(n\) readings is greater than \(0.97\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X>77)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z>\frac{77-68}{7}\right)=1-\Phi(1.28571)=0.0993.\]

Let \(r\) be the unrounded upper-tail probability.

\[\mathrm P(K<2)=(1-r)^{7}+7r(1-r)^{6}=0.852.\]

(b)

\[1-(1-r)^n>0.97\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad n>\frac{\ln(0.03)}{\ln(1-r)}=33.5391184.\]

The logarithm in the denominator is negative, so its sign must be considered when dividing.

\[\mathrm P(K\geq1)\big|_{n=33}=0.96826047,\quad\mathrm P(K\geq1)\big|_{n=34}=0.9714113.\]

Thus the first integer satisfying the strict condition is \(34\).

questions.title: One item from each production method
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability.

A strength measurement for method A is normally distributed with mean \(90\) and standard deviation \(8\). For method B it is normally distributed with mean \(72\) and standard deviation \(\sigma_B\). For method B, the proportion below \(66\) is \(0.25\). One item from each method is chosen independently.

  1. Find \(\sigma_B\).

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that the item from A exceeds \(82\) and the item from B does not.

    [3]

  3. Given that exactly one of the two items exceeds \(82\), find the probability that it is the item from A.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{66-72}{\sigma_B}=\Phi^{-1}(0.25),\qquad\sigma_B=8.90.\]

(b)

\[a=\mathrm P(X_A>82)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{82-90}{8}\right)=0.84134475.\]\[b=\mathrm P(X_B>82)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{82-72}{8.8956133}\right)=0.13047479.\]\[\mathrm P(X_A>82,X_B\leq 82)=a(1-b)=0.732.\]

(c)

Exactly one consists of two disjoint cases.

\[\frac{a(1-b)}{a(1-b)+(1-a)b}=0.972.\]
questions.hint_html: You need probabilities of two separate events, not the distribution of the sum or difference of the measurements.

marking_criteria.description_html: Selects the cumulative probability, including the correct tail.
Uses an appropriate inverse-normal equation with standard deviation.
Correct value.
Calculates both relevant normal probabilities.
Multiplies by independence, complementing the B event.
Correct joint probability.
Uses both cases in the conditioning event.

questions.title: A mixed stock of sensors
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability.

A stock contains sensors of types A and B. The probability that a randomly chosen sensor is type A is \(0.6\). Conditional on type A, its response \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm N(62,36)\); conditional on type B, it has distribution \(\mathrm N(70,81)\).

  1. Find the probability that the response of a randomly chosen sensor exceeds \(75\).

    [3]

  2. Given that the response exceeds \(75\), find the probability that the sensor is type B.

    [3]

  3. Explain why it is not valid simply to average the two means and standard deviations and treat the mixed stock as one normal distribution.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.125\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

\(0.927\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

The model is conditional on the sensor type. Its overall tail is a weighted sum of two normal tail probabilities; a single normal model with averaged parameters is not supplied or implied.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p_A=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{75-62}{6}\right)=0.01513014,\qquad p_B=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{75-70}{9}\right)=0.28925736.\]\[\mathrm P(X>75)=0.6p_A+0.4p_B=0.125.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(B\mid X>75)=\frac{0.4p_B}{0.6p_A+0.4p_B}=0.927.\]

(c)

Even the average standard deviation would not account for the difference between the two centres. The calculation must condition on the type and combine probabilities.

questions.title: A mixed stock of sensors
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability.

A stock contains sensors of types A and B. The probability that a randomly chosen sensor is type A is \(0.65\). Conditional on type A, its response \(X\) has distribution \(\mathrm N(88,64)\); conditional on type B, it has distribution \(\mathrm N(99,144)\).

  1. Find the probability that the response of a randomly chosen sensor exceeds \(105\).

    [3]

  2. Given that the response exceeds \(105\), find the probability that the sensor is type B.

    [3]

  3. Explain why it is not valid simply to average the two means and standard deviations and treat the mixed stock as one normal distribution.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.119\) (3 s.f.).

(b)

\(0.908\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

The model is conditional on the sensor type. Its overall tail is a weighted sum of two normal tail probabilities; a single normal model with averaged parameters is not supplied or implied.
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p_A=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{105-88}{8}\right)=0.01679331,\qquad p_B=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{105-99}{12}\right)=0.30853754.\]\[\mathrm P(X>105)=0.65p_A+0.35p_B=0.119.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(B\mid X>105)=\frac{0.35p_B}{0.65p_A+0.35p_B}=0.908.\]

(c)

Even the average standard deviation would not account for the difference between the two centres. The calculation must condition on the type and combine probabilities.

questions.title: Repeated sets of normal readings
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability; Binomial models and moments.

Independent readings are normally distributed with mean \(84\) and standard deviation \(8\). A reading above \(91\) is flagged. Each set contains \(6\) readings.

  1. Find the probability that exactly two readings in a set are flagged.

    [3]

  2. Given that a set has at least one flagged reading, find the probability that it has exactly two.

    [2]

  3. \(3\) independent sets are examined. Find the probability that at least one of the sets has exactly two flagged readings.

    [2]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X>91)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z>\frac{91-84}{8}\right)=1-\Phi(0.875)=0.191.\]

Let \(r\) be the unrounded flag probability.

\[\mathrm P(K=2)=\binom{6}2r^2(1-r)^{4}=0.234.\]

(b)

\[\mathrm P(K=2\mid K\geq1)=\frac{\mathrm P(K=2)}{1-(1-r)^{6}}=0.326.\]

(c)

The event for one set has probability \(q=\mathrm P(K=2)\). It is not the single-reading flag probability.

\[1-(1-q)^{3}=0.551.\]

questions.title: A measured batch and a finite selection
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Conditional probability.

A batch of \(800\) readings is modelled by a normal distribution with unknown mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(4.5\). Exactly \(200\) of these readings exceed \(50\).

  1. Use the observed proportion to estimate \(\mu\).

    [3]

  2. Three of these recorded readings are now selected uniformly without replacement. Find the exact probability that precisely two exceed \(50\). You may give a fraction or an exact product.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{50-\mu}{4.5}=\Phi^{-1}\!\left(1-\frac{200}{800}\right).\]\[\mu=50-4.5\Phi^{-1}(0.75)=47.0.\]

(b)

Use the observed finite counts, not a newly simulated normal sample. For the order exceed, exceed, do not exceed, multiply the changing fractions; the non-exceedance can occupy any of three places.

\[3\times\frac{200}{800}\times\frac{199}{799}\times\frac{600}{798}.\]

A binomial formula with the original proportion in every factor would ignore the lack of replacement.
questions.hint_html: The second experiment samples the actual recorded batch. Its composition is known and changes after each selection.

questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A performance measurement \(X\) is normally distributed. The proportions of measurements exceeding \(44\) and \(60\) are \(0.8\) and \(0.15\), respectively. Measurements on different items are independent.

  1. Find the mean and standard deviation.

    [5]

  2. A random sample of \(8\) items is taken. Find the probability that at least two have measurements greater than \(63\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{44-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.2)=-0.841621,\qquad\frac{60-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.85)=1.036433.\]

Subtract the first equation from the second before finding the mean. Keep the signs of both quantiles.

\[\sigma=\frac{16}{1.036433-(-0.841621)}=8.52,\qquad\mu=44-\sigma(-0.841621)=51.2.\]

Unrounded values are retained in the following calculations.

(b)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X>63)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z>\frac{63-51.1701534}{8.51945402}\right)=1-\Phi(1.38857)=0.0825.\]

Retain the unrounded exceedance probability \(r\) from the fitted model. The count in the sample is \(\mathrm B(8,r)\).

\[\mathrm P(K\geq2)=1-(1-r)^{8}-8r(1-r)^{7}=0.137.\]

questions.title: A count between inclusive limits
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

Each of \(240\) independent orders requires a special attachment with probability \(0.58\). Let \(Y\) be the number requiring the attachment.

  1. State a suitable approximating normal distribution and justify its use.

    [2]

  2. Use this approximation to find \(\mathrm P(128\leq Y\leq 149)\).

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[np=139.2>5,\qquad n(1-p)=100.8>5.\]

Both expected counts are sufficiently large. The variance is \(np(1-p)=58.464\).

(b)

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(240,0.58)\). Since \(np=139.2>5\) and \(n(1-p)=100.8>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(139.2,58.464)\).

\[\mathrm P(128\leq Y\leq 149)\simeq\mathrm P(127.5<W<149.5).\]\[=\Phi\!\left(\frac{149.5-139.2}{\sqrt{58.464}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{127.5-139.2}{\sqrt{58.464}}\right)=0.848.\]
questions.hint_html: Both end counts are included, so the continuous interval extends half a unit beyond each.

questions.title: Fewer than a specified count
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A stored file is selected for inspection with probability \(0.28\), independently of other files. There are \(200\) files. Let \(Y\) count those selected.

  1. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that fewer than \(62\) files are selected.

    [4]

  2. Use the same normal approximation to estimate the probability that exactly \(62\) files are selected.

    [3]

(a)

Since the count is an integer, \(Y<62\) means \(Y\leq61\).

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(200,0.28)\). Since \(np=56>5\) and \(n(1-p)=144>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(56,40.32)\).

Include the whole bar for the largest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 61)\simeq\mathrm P(W<61.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{61.5-56}{\sqrt{40.32}}\right)=0.807.\]

(b)

An exact discrete count corresponds to a bar of width one, not one point under a continuous curve.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(200,0.28)\). Since \(np=56>5\) and \(n(1-p)=144>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(56,40.32)\).

\[\mathrm P(62\leq Y\leq 62)\simeq\mathrm P(61.5<W<62.5).\]\[=\Phi\!\left(\frac{62.5-56}{\sqrt{40.32}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{61.5-56}{\sqrt{40.32}}\right)=0.0402.\]

questions.title: When a normal approximation is suitable
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A diagnostic flag appears independently on each trial with probability \(0.12\).

  1. For \(15\) trials, explain why a normal approximation is not appropriate for the number of flags.

    [1]

  2. Find the exact probability of at most two flags in \(15\) trials. Give an exact expression or an answer to 3 significant figures.

    [3]

  3. For \(250\) trials, use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability of no more than \(38\) flags.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The expected number of flags is \(1.8\), which is not greater than 5.

(b)

\(0.735\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

\(0.951\) (3 s.f.).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[np=15\times0.12=1.8<5.\]

A large expected number of non-flags alone does not meet both conditions.

(b)

\[\sum_{r=0}^2\binom{15}r(0.12)^r(0.88)^{15-r}=0.735.\]

(c)

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(250,0.12)\). Since \(np=30>5\) and \(n(1-p)=220>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(30,26.4)\).

Include the whole bar for the largest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 38)\simeq\mathrm P(W<38.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{38.5-30}{\sqrt{26.4}}\right)=0.951.\]

questions.title: When a normal approximation is suitable
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A diagnostic flag appears independently on each trial with probability \(0.15\).

  1. For \(12\) trials, explain why a normal approximation is not appropriate for the number of flags.

    [1]

  2. Find the exact probability of at most two flags in \(12\) trials. Give an exact expression or an answer to 3 significant figures.

    [3]

  3. For \(280\) trials, use a suitable normal approximation to find the probability of no more than \(50\) flags.

    [4]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

The expected number of flags is \(1.8\), which is not greater than 5.

(b)

\(0.736\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

\(0.923\) (3 s.f.).
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[np=12\times0.15=1.8<5.\]

A large expected number of non-flags alone does not meet both conditions.

(b)

\[\sum_{r=0}^2\binom{12}r(0.15)^r(0.85)^{12-r}=0.736.\]

(c)

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(280,0.15)\). Since \(np=42>5\) and \(n(1-p)=238>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(42,35.7)\).

Include the whole bar for the largest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 50)\simeq\mathrm P(W<50.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{50.5-42}{\sqrt{35.7}}\right)=0.923.\]

Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

Each independent delivery is assigned to one of three routes, A, B or C. The probabilities of routes A and B are \(0.25\) and \(0.18\), respectively. In a sample of \(250\) deliveries, \(Y\) is the number using route C.

  1. Find the probability that a delivery uses route C.

    [1]

  2. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that at least \(148\) deliveries use route C.

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 148)\simeq\mathrm P(W>147.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{147.5-142.5}{\sqrt{61.275}}\right)=0.261.\]
questions.hint_html: The three routes are mutually exclusive and exhaustive. The count concerns the third route.

questions.title: Weighted outputs from a generator
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A random generator produces one of the symbols A, B, C and D. Their probabilities are in the ratio \(3:2:5:4\), respectively. Outputs are independent. Symbols B and D are called selected outputs.

  1. Find the probability of a selected output.

    [1]

  2. Find the probability that exactly two of four outputs are selected.

    [2]

  3. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that more than \(135\) of \(300\) outputs are selected.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[p=\frac{2+4}{14}=0.428571429.\]

(b)

\[\binom42 p^2(1-p)^2=0.360.\]

(c)

More than 135 means at least 136.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(300,0.42857143)\). Since \(np=128.57143>5\) and \(n(1-p)=171.42857>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(128.571429,73.469388)\).

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 136)\simeq\mathrm P(W>135.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{135.5-128.571429}{\sqrt{73.469388}}\right)=0.209.\]
questions.hint_html: The combined probability for B and D must be normalised by the sum of all four weights.

questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

For a continuous response time \(T\), \(\mathrm P(T<8)=0.14\) and \(\mathrm P(T<16)=0.82\). Response times are independent. A response is classified as intermediate when it lies between \(8\) and \(16\).

  1. Find the probability of an intermediate response.

    [1]

  2. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that more than \(200\) of \(280\) responses are intermediate.

    [4]

  3. Does the calculation in part (b) require the response time itself to be normally distributed? Explain.

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(0.68\).

(b)

\(0.0978\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

No. The intermediate/not-intermediate indicators form a binomial count. The normal approximation is applied to that count, not to the original response time.

(a)

\[p=0.82-0.14=0.68.\]

(b)

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(280,0.68)\). Since \(np=190.4>5\) and \(n(1-p)=89.6>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(190.4,60.928)\).

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 201)\simeq\mathrm P(W>200.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{200.5-190.4}{\sqrt{60.928}}\right)=0.0978.\]

(c)

Only the interval probability, independence and a fixed number of trials are needed for this binomial model. The two given cumulative probabilities do not identify the full distribution of T.

questions.title: From a dimensional limit to a batch count
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

The width \(X\) mm of a clip is normally distributed with mean \(22\) mm and standard deviation \(1.8\) mm. A clip fits a slot when its width is less than \(24\) mm. Different clips have independent widths.

  1. Find the probability that one clip fits the slot.

    [3]

  2. A random batch contains \(240\) clips. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that at least \(210\) fit. Justify the approximation.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

The standard deviation, rather than the variance, is used in the denominator.

\[\mathrm P(X<24)=\mathrm P\!\left(Z<\frac{24-22}{1.8}\right)=\Phi(1.11111)=0.867.\]

A normally distributed measurement \(X\) has mean \(5.4\) and standard deviation \(0.7\). An item is suitable for a particular use when \(4.5<X<5\). Measurements on different items are independent.

  1. Find the probability that one item is suitable.

    [3]

  2. Find the probability that at least two of \(5\) items are suitable. Use the exact binomial model.

    [3]

  3. Use a normal approximation to estimate the probability that fewer than \(60\) of \(300\) items are suitable.

(a)

Let \(p\) be the unrounded suitability probability.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(300,0.18458319)\). Since \(np=55.37496>5\) and \(n(1-p)=244.62504>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(55.374956,45.15367)\).

Include the whole bar for the largest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 59)\simeq\mathrm P(W<59.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{59.5-55.374956}{\sqrt{45.15367}}\right)=0.730.\]

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 55)\simeq\mathrm P(W<55.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{55.5-57.609979}{\sqrt{39.171592}}\right)=0.368.\]

questions.title: Counting batches with a particular composition
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A batch contains \(8\) independent items. Each item passes a test with probability \(0.64\). A batch is classified as type R if exactly \(5\) items pass. Results for different batches are independent.

  1. Find the probability that a batch is type R.

    [3]

  2. Use a suitable approximation to find the probability that no more than \(75\) of \(260\) batches are type R. Justify your approximation.

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[q=\binom{8}{5}(0.64)^{5}(0.36)^{3}=0.281.\]

(b)

The outer binomial success is an entire batch of type R, with probability \(q\), not a single item passing.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(260,0.28054039)\). Since \(np=72.9405>5\) and \(n(1-p)=187.0595>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(72.940502,52.477745)\).

Include the whole bar for the largest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\leq 75)\simeq\mathrm P(W<75.5)=\Phi\!\left(\frac{75.5-72.940502}{\sqrt{52.477745}}\right)=0.638.\]
questions.hint_html: First calculate the probability for one whole batch. That becomes the success probability of the second count.

questions.title: A lower planning guarantee for rejected batches
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

Each batch contains \(20\) independent components, each faulty with probability \(0.08\). A batch is rejected if it contains at least \(3\) faulty components. Batches are independent. A shipment contains \(200\) batches, and \(Y\) is the number rejected.

  1. Find the probability that one batch is rejected.

    [3]

  2. Using a continuity-corrected normal approximation, find the greatest integer \(k\) for which \(\mathrm P(Y\geq k)\geq 0.95\).

    [5]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[q=1-\sum_{t=0}^{2}\binom{20}t(0.08)^t(0.92)^{20-t}=0.212.\]

(b)

Use the unrounded batch-rejection probability. Both expected counts exceed five.

\[Y\approx\mathrm N(42.4107508,33.4173919).\]\[1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{k-0.5-42.4107508}{5.7807778}\right)\geq 0.95.\]\[k\leq 42.4107508+0.5+5.7807778\Phi^{-1}(0.05)=33.4022175.\]\[\widehat{\mathrm P}(Y\geq 33)=0.9567753,\qquad\widehat{\mathrm P}(Y\geq 34)=0.9383957.\]

The greatest integer allowed by this approximation is \(33\). This is an approximation-based planning threshold, not a claim about an exact binomial quantile.
questions.hint_html: A larger proposed lower count makes the guarantee harder to satisfy, so the required integer is obtained by rounding the derived bound down.

questions.title: A linked-parameter model and an interval count
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

Independent values of \(X\) have a normal distribution with \(\mu=3\sigma\) and \(\sigma>0\). It is known that \(\mathrm P(X>30)=0.06\).

  1. Find \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(18<X<30)\).

    [3]

  3. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that at least \(142\) of \(250\) observations lie in this interval.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{30-3\sigma}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.94).\]\[\sigma=\frac{30}{3+\Phi^{-1}(0.94)}=6.59,\qquad\mu=3\sigma=19.8.\]

(b)

Standardise using \(Z=\frac{X-19.75948928}{6.58649643}\).

\[\mathrm P(18<X<30)=\Phi(1.55477)-\Phi(-0.26714)=0.545.\]

(c)

Use the interval probability, not the given upper-tail probability, for this count.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(250,0.54531771)\). Since \(np=136.32943>5\) and \(n(1-p)=113.67057>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(136.329429,61.986576)\).

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 142)\simeq\mathrm P(W>141.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{141.5-136.329429}{\sqrt{61.986576}}\right)=0.256.\]
questions.hint_html: After fitting the model, calculate the interval probability before defining the binomial count.

questions.title: A linked-parameter model and an interval count
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

Independent values of \(X\) have a normal distribution with \(\mu=4.5\sigma\) and \(\sigma>0\). It is known that \(\mathrm P(X>60)=0.07\).

  1. Find \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

    [3]

  2. Find \(\mathrm P(39<X<60)\).

    [3]

  3. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that at least \(271\) of \(400\) observations lie in this interval.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{60-4.5\sigma}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.93).\]\[\sigma=\frac{60}{4.5+\Phi^{-1}(0.93)}=10.0,\qquad\mu=4.5\sigma=45.2.\]

(b)

Standardise using \(Z=\frac{X-45.18230285}{10.04051174}\).

\[\mathrm P(39<X<60)=\Phi(1.47579)-\Phi(-0.61574)=0.661.\]

(c)

Use the interval probability, not the given upper-tail probability, for this count.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(400,0.66096556)\). Since \(np=264.38622>5\) and \(n(1-p)=135.61378>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(264.386223,89.636036)\).

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 271)\simeq\mathrm P(W>270.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{270.5-264.386223}{\sqrt{89.636036}}\right)=0.259.\]

questions.title: Choosing a sample size for a count guarantee
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments; Quadratic equations and valid roots.

Each independent attempt succeeds with probability \(0.72\). Let \(Y\) be the number of successes in \(n\) attempts. Use a continuity-corrected normal approximation throughout this question.

  1. Find the least integer \(n\) for which the approximated probability of at least \(80\) successes is at least \(0.95\). Check the two neighbouring integer sample sizes.

    [6]

  2. For this value of \(n\), estimate the probability of exactly \(80\) successes.

    [3]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[Y\approx\mathrm N(0.72n,0.2016n).\]\[1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{79.5-0.72n}{\sqrt{0.2016n}}\right)\geq0.95.\]\[0.72n-79.5\geq\Phi^{-1}(0.95)\sqrt{0.2016n}.\]

Put \(t=\sqrt n>0\). This gives a quadratic inequality in \(t\), with one positive boundary root. The inequality holds above that root.

\[0.72t^2-0.73853745t-79.5\geq0.\]\[n\geq 121.73405092.\]\[\widehat{\mathrm P}(Y\geq80)\big|_{n=121}=0.93856353,\quad\widehat{\mathrm P}(Y\geq80)\big|_{n=122}=0.95368361.\]

Both expected successes and expected failures exceed five at these sample sizes. The least integer under the requested approximation is \(122\).

(b)

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(122,0.72)\). Since \(np=87.84>5\) and \(n(1-p)=34.16>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(87.84,24.5952)\).

\[\mathrm P(80\leq Y\leq 80)\simeq\mathrm P(79.5<W<80.5).\]\[=\Phi\!\left(\frac{80.5-87.84}{\sqrt{24.5952}}\right)-\Phi\!\left(\frac{79.5-87.84}{\sqrt{24.5952}}\right)=0.0231.\]
questions.hint_html: After correcting the lower count boundary, use a normal quantile. A substitution t=sqrt(n) avoids introducing an incorrect sign by squaring.

The random variable \(Y\) is binomial with unknown parameters \(n\) and \(p\). Its mean is \(72\) and its variance is \(43.2\).

    [4]

    [1]
questions.answer_html:
(a)

\(n=180,\quad p=0.4\).

(b)

\(0.890\) (3 s.f.).

(c)

That number is the variance. Standardisation divides by its positive square root, the standard deviation.

(c)

(c)

\[Z=\frac{W-90}{\sqrt{57.6}}.\]

questions.title: Calibration data and a batch acceptance rule
questions.prompt_html:
Mixed-topic prerequisite: Binomial models and moments.

A continuous test measurement \(X\) is normally distributed with unknown mean \(\mu\) and standard deviation \(\sigma\). It is known that \(\mathrm P(X<42)=0.1\) and \(\mathrm P(X>68)=0.15\). An item passes when \(40\leq X\leq 70\). Measurements on different items are independent.

  1. Find \(\mu\) and \(\sigma\).

    [5]

  2. Find the probability that an item passes.

    [3]

  3. A batch of \(400\) items is accepted if at least \(336\) pass. Use a normal approximation to find the probability that a batch is accepted.

    [4]
questions.solution_html:
(a)

\[\frac{42-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.1)=-1.281552,\qquad\frac{68-\mu}{\sigma}=\Phi^{-1}(0.85)=1.036433.\]

Subtract the first equation from the second before finding the mean. Keep the signs of both quantiles.

\[\sigma=\frac{26}{1.036433-(-1.281552)}=11.2,\qquad\mu=42-\sigma(-1.281552)=56.4.\]

Unrounded values are retained in the following calculations.

(b)

The new acceptance limits are not the original calibration boundaries. Use both fitted parameters without rounding.

Standardise using \(Z=\frac{X-56.37470102}{11.21663881}\).

\[\mathrm P(40<X<70)=\Phi(1.21474)-\Phi(-1.45986)=0.816.\]

(c)

Let \(Y\) count passing items. Its success probability is the interval probability from part (b), not either calibration tail. Keep this probability unrounded.

Let \(Y\) count the relevant outcomes. Then \(Y\sim\mathrm B(400,0.81560281)\). Since \(np=326.24112>5\) and \(n(1-p)=73.75888>5\), use \(W\sim\mathrm N(326.241125,60.157946)\).

Include the whole bar for the smallest permitted integer.

\[\mathrm P(Y\geq 336)\simeq\mathrm P(W>335.5)=1-\Phi\!\left(\frac{335.5-326.241125}{\sqrt{60.157946}}\right)=0.116.\]
questions.hint_html: Fit the individual measurement model, obtain the new pass probability, and only then define the binomial batch count.
